w:r.w:t: DEPARTMENT OF COMPUTER AND SOFTWARE ENGINEERING
Altera Quartus II: FPGA Design with SystemVerilog
Simulation & Implementation of a Single-Cycle MIPS Processor

Altera Quartus II is a comprehensive design software suite developed by Altera Corporation (now Intel) for the design, simulation, synthesis, and implementation of digital circuits on CPLD (Complex Programmable Logic Device) and FPGA (Field Programmable Gate Array) platforms. Quartus II provides an integrated environment that supports multiple Hardware Description Languages (HDLs), including VHDL, Verilog, SystemVerilog, and schematic-based entry.

In this lab, we use Quartus II version 13.1 (64-bit) Web Edition — a free version suitable for academic and small-scale FPGA design. The target device family used is Cyclone IV E (EP4CE115F29C7), a high-performance FPGA from Altera with 114,480 logic elements, widely used in embedded systems design.

The circuit implemented in this lab is a complete Single-Cycle MIPS processor described in SystemVerilog HDL, based on the architecture presented in Patterson & Hennessy, “Computer Organization and Design” (2014), Appendix B. The MIPS processor executes each instruction in exactly one clock cycle and supports the following instruction types: R-type (ADD, SUB, AND, OR, SLT), memory instructions (LW, SW), branch instructions (BEQ), and jump instructions (J).
This lab report covers all eight sections of the Altera Quartus II Tutorial as applied to the MIPS processor design:

Starting a New Project — Creating Quartus II projects for each design component.
Synthesizing the Design — Compiling and synthesizing all SystemVerilog modules.
Inspecting Synthesis Results — Reviewing Compilation Reports and the datapath block diagram.

The MIPS (Microprocessor without Interlocked Pipeline Stages) architecture is a 32-bit RISC (Reduced Instruction Set Computer) design. In a single-cycle implementation, each instruction fetches, decodes, executes, and writes back results within one clock period. The processor datapath consists of the following key sub-modules:
Program Counter (PC) — 32-bit register holding the current instruction address.
Instruction Memory (imem) — 64-word read-only ROM pre-loaded with the test program.
Register File (regfile) — 32 general-purpose 32-bit registers ($zero hardwired to 0).
32-bit ALU (alu_32bit) — performs AND, OR, ADD, SUB, SLT, NOR operations.
ALU Control Unit (alu_control) — decodes ALUOp[1:0] and funct[5:0] to ALUcontrol[2:0].
Main Decoder (maindec) — decodes 6-bit opcode to 9 control signals.
Data Memory (dmem) — 64-word synchronous RAM for LW/SW instructions.
Sign Extender (sign_extend) — extends 16-bit immediate to 32 bits.
Multiplexers — mux2to1 instances selecting ALUSrc, RegDst, MemToReg, PCSrc.

The ALU is the computational core of the MIPS datapath. It performs six operations selected by a 3-bit ALUcontrol signal. Subtraction is implemented using 2's complement arithmetic: when ALUcontrol[2]=1, operand B is bitwise-inverted and a carry-in of 1 is added, which is equivalent to negating B. The zero flag supports BEQ branch decisions.
assign b_mux = ALUcontrol[2] ? (~b) : b; // invert for SUB/SLT
assign {, sum} = a + b_mux + ALUcontrol[2]; // 2's complement add

The top-level mips_processor module integrates all sub-modules into a complete single-cycle datapath. The main decoder (maindec) decodes the 6-bit opcode to generate 9 control signals. The ALU control unit (alu_control) performs a two-level decode using ALUOp[1:0] and the funct field from R-type instructions.

After a successful compilation, Quartus II provides several tools to inspect the synthesis results. This section describes the key results examined in the Compilation Report, the datapath block diagram, and the timing analysis for all four design modules.
The Compilation Report Flow Summary was accessed for each module by opening Processing > Compilation Report after each successful build. The key results are:

The Compilation Report Flow Summary confirms the target device as EP4CE115F29C7 — a Cyclone IV E FPGA with 114,480 logic elements and 529 available I/O pins. The utilization breakdown for the complete MIPS processor is:
Total logic elements: 4,010 / 114,480 (4%) — combinational logic for ALU, control, and MUX structures.
Total combinational functions: 2,567 / 114,480 (2%) — purely combinational blocks.
Dedicated logic registers: 3,102 / 114,480 (3%) — register file (32×32=1,024 bits) + data memory (64×32=2,048 bits) + PC register (32 bits).
Total pins: 162 / 529 (31%) — clk, reset, and I/O for the processor interface.
Total memory bits: 0 — memories are implemented in logic elements, not dedicated memory blocks.
The ALU uses 173 logic elements — all combinational. The Fitter maps the 6-operation ALU as follows:
ADD/SUB: 32 full-adder chains using carry-chain primitives (32 LEs for the adder).
AND/OR/NOR: Bitwise operations mapped to LE look-up tables (32 LEs each per operation).
SLT: Uses the MSB of the subtraction result (sum[31]) to determine the less-than comparison.
Zero flag: 32-bit NOR reduction to check if result equals zero.

Key observations: (1) ADDI at cycles 1–2 loads 5 and 10 into $t0/$t1 — values appear as decimal numbers on the waveform bars. (2) ADD at cycle 3 gives $t2=15 (5+10), ALUcontrol=010. (3) SUB at cycle 4 gives $t3=5 (10−5), ALUcontrol=110. (4) ANDI at cycle 5 gives $t4=1 (0101₂ & 0011₂ = 0001₂), ALUcontrol=000. (5) SW writes $t2=15 to Mem[0] (memwrite=1). (6) LW at cycle 7 reads Mem[0]=15 into $s0 (memtoreg=1). (7) BEQ at cycle 8 detects $t0==$t0 (zero=1, pcsrc=1) and jumps to PC=0x24.

I-type ADDI: imm=5 sign-extended, added to $zero; alusrc=1, regwrite=1, regdst=0
I-type ADDI: loads constant 10; visible as decimal on waveform bar from this cycle
R-type ADD: ALUcontrol=010; regdst=1 (rd=destination), alusrc=0 (register B used)
R-type SUB: ALUcontrol=110; two’s complement, B inverted then +1 added
SW: ALU addr=0+0=0; memwrite=1, writedata=$t2=15 written to data memory word 0
LW: addr=0, readdata=0x0F=15; memtoreg=1 routes memory read to register write-back
BEQ: ALU computes $t0−$t0=0, zero=1, pcsrc=1; PC+12=0x24 (NOP at 0x20 skipped)
Post-branch idle; registers and memory hold final values: $t0=5,$t1=10,$t2=15,$s0=15

Simulation verifies the functional correctness of the design before committing to FPGA synthesis. The mips_processor.sv file includes an integrated testbench (mips_processor_tb) that exercises the pre-loaded 10-instruction test program stored in the instruction memory.
The instruction memory (imem) is pre-loaded with the following 10-instruction MIPS test program. Register initial values: $t0=5, $t1=12, $t3=7, $t4=3, and data memory initialized.

The simulation uses the integrated testbench within mips_processor.sv. The testbench applies a clock with a 10 ns period and holds reset active for the first 22 ns to initialize the processor. After de-asserting reset, the PC advances by 4 each clock cycle, executing one instruction per cycle.
For functional simulation using Quartus II Simulator:
A Vector Waveform File (VWF) is created via File > New > Verification/Debugging Files > University Program VWF.
Signals clk, reset, pc[31:0], instr[31:0], aluout[31:0], zero are added using the Node Finder (Filter: Pins: All).
The clock is set to 10 ns period. Reset is driven high for 0–20 ns then low.
The functional simulation netlist is generated via Processing > Generate Functional Simulation Netlist.
Simulation is started via Processing > Start Simulation.
The simulation confirms correct operation of all instruction types. Key observations from the waveform:
Clock cycle 1 (PC=0): add instruction — ALU output = 17 (0x00000011), zero=0. Write to $t2 on next rising edge.
Clock cycle 2 (PC=4): sub instruction — ALU computes 7−3=4 using 2's complement. ALU output = 4, zero=0.
Clock cycle 3 (PC=8): and instruction — ALU output = 5 & 12 = 4 (0b0101 & 0b1100 = 0b0100).
Clock cycle 4 (PC=12): or instruction — ALU output = 5 | 12 = 13 (0b1101).
Clock cycle 5 (PC=16): slt instruction — 7 is NOT less than 3, so result=0, zero=1.
Clock cycle 6 (PC=20): lw instruction — memory address = $t0+4 = 9, reads Mem[9].
Clock cycle 7 (PC=24): sw instruction — Mem[5] is written with $s0=4. MemWrite=1.
Clock cycle 8 (PC=28): beq instruction — $t0==$t0 so zero=1, branch taken. PC jumps to 44.
The one-clock-cycle execution model is confirmed: each instruction completes within exactly one clock cycle, with register writes on the rising edge following the combinational computation.

Pin assignments specify which physical I/O pins on the FPGA device correspond to each signal in the design. Correct pin assignments are essential for physically implementing the circuit on a development board. Quartus II provides three methods for making pin assignments.

The Assignment Editor is accessed via Assignments > Assignment Editor. In the Category field, “Pin” was selected. For each signal, the physical pin location is assigned by double-clicking in the Location column. The clock signal (clk) must be assigned to a dedicated clock pin (e.g., PIN_Y2 on the DE2 board) to ensure low-skew distribution through the global clock network.

The Pin Planner provides a graphical view of the FPGA package (FBGA-780 for EP4CE115F29C7) and allows drag-and-drop pin assignment. It is accessed via Assignments > Pin Planner. The device package diagram shows all 529 I/O pins organized by I/O banks.

Pin assignments can also be imported from a CSV file using Assignments > Import Assignments. For the Altera DE2 development board, a pre-made pin assignment file (DE2_pin_assignments.csv) is available from the Altera website.

If a Cyclone IV E development board (such as the Altera DE2-115 board) were available, the MIPS processor circuit would be physically programmed onto the FPGA using the following steps:
Connect the DE2-115 development board to the computer via USB-Blaster cable and power it on.
In Quartus II, open the Programmer by selecting Tools > Programmer (or clicking the Programmer icon in the toolbar).
The Programmer window shows Hardware Setup as “USB-Blaster [USB-0]”, Mode as “JTAG”, and the programming file as mips_processor.sof (SRAM Object File) with the Program/Configure checkbox checked.
Click Start to program the device. The progress bar reaches 100% and a success message “Configuration Succeeded” appears.
After programming, the clock can be driven by the 50 MHz crystal oscillator on the DE2-115 board (PIN_Y2). The reset signal is mapped to a pushbutton (KEY[0]).
The processor outputs (PC address, ALU result, memory write data) can be monitored on the seven-segment displays or LEDs of the DE2-115 board.

The compiled programming file mips_processor.sof was generated successfully in the mips/db/ directory during the full compilation flow, confirming that the design is physically implementable on the Cyclone IV E target device.

The Fitter Equations represent the actual logic circuit implemented by Quartus II on the FPGA device. These equations describe exactly how the logic elements (LEs) and flip-flops in the Cyclone IV E FPGA are configured to realize the MIPS processor design. They can be viewed in the Compilation Report under Fitter > Equations.

8.2 Flip-Flop Primitives in the MIPS Processor
The MIPS processor contains three types of registered elements, each inferred from clocked always blocks in the SystemVerilog code:
PC Register (32 D flip-flops): The PC always @(posedge clk) block infers 32 DFFs for the program counter. Each flip-flop uses the DFFEAS primitive with asynchronous reset (CLRN).
Register File (1,024 D flip-flops): The 32×32-bit register file always @(posedge clk) write block infers 1,024 DFFs. Register $zero is not synthesized (it is always zero and optimized away).
Data Memory (2,048 D flip-flops): The 64×32-bit dmem always @(posedge clk) block infers 2,048 DFFs for data storage.
8.3 Example Fitter Equations for the MIPS Processor

After successful compilation, the Fitter equations for the PC register appear as follows. Each bit of the 32-bit PC is implemented as a separate DFFEAS (D flip-flop with synchronous/asynchronous controls):
; Each bit is a DFFEAS with GLOBAL clock and active-low reset
pc[0] = DFFEAS(pcnext[0], GLOBAL(clk), !reset, VCC, VCC, GND, GND, GND, GND)
pc[1] = DFFEAS(pcnext[1], GLOBAL(clk), !reset, VCC, VCC, GND, GND, GND, GND)
pc[31] = DFFEAS(pcnext[31], GLOBAL(clk), !reset, VCC, VCC, GND, GND, GND, GND)
